text:
A newly proposed legislative measure would require all school districts in Virginia to employ a licensed nurse in every school. (Stock photo Sewcream Studio/Getty Images)Virginia schools could be required to have a licensed nurse in every building starting in 2028, under a legislative proposal introduced Wednesday. The measure is designed to close healthcare gaps by placing experts in schools to manage complex medical conditions.
Virginia permits school divisions to employ nurses, but state law doesn’t require it. About 8% of Virginia’s schools operate without a nurse.
At the School Health Services Committee’s Wednesday meeting, speakers and committee members supported the proposal. As written, it offers districts facing nurse shortages two-year waivers if they can show they made a good-faith effort to hire.
“School nursing is public health,” said Paula Nichols, school health administrator at Washington County Public Schools, during a video call on Wednesday. 
She said during Hurricane Helene, school nurses helped serve whole communities, not just students during the school day, going door to door to bring cases of water and medical care while wading through high water.
They also helped run community supply drives with other local partners.
“When the next emergency comes, and we know they always do, we need those relationships already in place,” Nichols said.
The proposed policy would require each school board to provide at least one licensed school nurse per building or per 325 students. The requirements would not take effect until July 1, 2028.
Schools have to compete with hospitals, clinics, academic institutions and nursing homes for nurses, according to workforce data collected by the Virginia Department of Health Professions.
Stacy Haynie, a lobbyist representing the Virginia School Board Association, supported the goal of having nurses in school buildings but raised concerns about implementing such a mandate because of a persistent shortage of nurses statewide. 
She noted that even when school boards want to hire nurses, they lack applicants for those positions.
“Regardless of what this committee does with this particular proposed legislation, I think we need to make sure that we don’t lose sight of the fact that there is a shortage of nurses across the commonwealth.”
Senate Education and Health Committee Chair Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, who also chairs the state’s school health services committee, said lawmakers are working to address the shortage.
She also backed the school nurse proposal, calling it a compromise and the main reason the committee was formed. 
“At the end of the day, we have to allow our teachers and school administrators to teach and manage the school, and having a nurse allows them to do their job,” Favola said. “A nurse is there to help with health issues that more and more of our children are facing every day.”
Betsy Looney, a committee member, said, “school nursing is not band-aids and ice packs,” emphasizing the central role nurses play in school safety.
“A nurse in every public school is not an additional service layered into the educational system,” Looney said. “It is the professional infrastructure necessary to safely and effectively implement the health responsibilities Virginia has already placed on its schools.” 
The committee will vote whether to send the proposal to the General Assembly for the upcoming session starting in January at its next business meeting on Nov. 18.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Changes could be coming to Blueprint education plan
description: The board overseeing implementation of Maryland's sweeping education reform plan could propose some changes to the plan, as another looming budget shortfall makes it a likely target for cuts to some lawmakers next year.
text:
Koen Hawk, a third grade student at Arbutus Elementary School in Baltimore County, colors on the first day of school Aug. 31. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The board overseeing implementation of Maryland’s sweeping education reform plan could propose some changes to the plan, as another looming budget shortfall makes it a likely target for cuts to some lawmakers next year.
A few of the changes being eyed by that Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board include adding more pathways for educators to achieve National Board Certification or other academic accreditation; providing funding for more college and career readiness classes; and conducting a study to assess how much to increase the base level of per pupil funding.
Those recommendations and more were discussed by board members at their meeting last week and could be finalized when the board meets again next month.
They come as the state faces a projected $3 billion budget gap for the upcoming fiscal year, about $1.8 billion of which is tied to education under the Blueprint, according to the Maryland Associations of Counties (MACo).
The projected budget shortfall for fiscal 2028 also comes in the first year in which Blueprint costs will exceed dedicated revenues. To cover the balance, the state will have to dip into the general fund, as a first-in-the-nation digital ad tax meant to help pay for the education plan remains in legal limbo.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Wednesday praised the Blueprint due to the work of educators and state Superintendent Carey Wright, such as improving math and reading test scores. But he also said, at the J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield, that “we have to be able to take a look at the Blueprint to ensure that all these things are not just effective but also scalable.”
“Our remarkable educators are helping to lead what has been one of the greatest rebounds post-COVID of any state inside of the United States of America,” Moore said. “This is some of the best work that’s happening in the country right now, and we want to make sure we’re continuing to support that.”
Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Lower Shore) at J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield Wednesday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Lower Shore) said she will work in the upcoming legislative session on proposing legislation to bring more flexibility under the Blueprint for the state’s 24 school districts.
That could include, for example, changes that would let a school district use resources or funding for prekindergarten that may be designated for career and technical education (CTE) in a district is already “doing well in CTE.”
“In other words, instead of that one-size-fits-all mandate, we go to the locals and work with them in good faith knowing that we have the same goal, which is a quality education for all students,” she said.
“We are facing very serious, long-term fiscal budget challenges,” Carozza said at Tawes. “So therefore, we’re going to work a little bit more with the individual counties, the school systems, so we can have a win-win.”
Legislative recommendations
The Blueprint board met Sept. 17 to review proposed legislative recommendations, which would ultimately need approval by the legislature.
One recommendation in the 15-page document would be to ease certification requirements for private providers who employ educators who teach prekindergarten students.
Such a change could build on House Bill 748, sponsored this year by Montgomery County Democratic Dels. Bernice Mireku-North and Julie Palakovich Carr, that creates another pathway for individuals to qualify as an early childhood teaching assistant. The law went into effect July 1.
Not all the possible changes are cost savings. Another recommendation is to require that multilingual learners and students with disabilities automatically receive Tier I funding, which provides free full-day prekindergarten for families at or below 300% of the Federal Poverty Level, or those experiencing homelessness. That policy had been in place from fiscal years 2024 to 2026.
“So making this change permanent will have a fiscal impact,” said Joy Schaefer, government relations director for the AIB.
Another recommendation would be to conduct a study on the impact of National Board Certification for teachers, especially in “high-need student populations.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The Learning Policy Institute, a national education research organization headquartered in San Francisco, recommended in a March report that policies should provide salary increases for teachers who receive not only advanced credentials, but also teach in subjects like special education or in rural and high-poverty schools. In February, the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards said Maryland led the nation last year with 1,435 of those teachers who received that designation.
The Blueprint currently requires that teachers who get National Board Certification get a $10,000 salary boost, and another $7,000 for those who teach at an “identified low-performing school.”
Not all local school officials are fans of the automatic pay bumps. Worcester County Superintendent Annette Wallace said last month that she vehemently disagrees with the Blueprint salary requirement.
“There’s no data in Worcester County Public Schools to suggest that National Board Certification makes you more of an effective teacher,” Wallace said in an interview last month. “Just because you’ve been teaching a long time doesn’t mean that you’re a great teacher. Quality is what’s more important to me, not number of years.”
The Blueprint board could vote on the legislative recommendations Oct. 15.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Underly says it’s urgent to fix the school funding formula but timing will depend on the election
description: Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly called for the state to overhaul the school funding formula in her sixth State of Education address Thursday, saying that the state “simply cannot afford to wait any longer.”  Underly delivered the address less than six weeks before the November election, when Wisconsin voters will decide who she will be […]
text:
“The formula used for funding our schools, for years, has failed our children, schools and entire communities,” Underly said during her address. Underly speaks to reporters after delivering her sixth State of Education address.  (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner) Wisconsin State Superintendent Jill Underly called for the state to overhaul the school funding formula in her sixth State of Education address Thursday, saying that the state “simply cannot afford to wait any longer.” 
Underly delivered the address less than six weeks before the November election, when Wisconsin voters will decide who she will be working with in the governor’s office and in the state Legislature on the next state budget. She will need their support to get the funding for the budget proposals she has begun to formulate.
The Department of Public Instruction so far has only submitted the first part of its budget request, which covered funding for libraries, support for children who are deaf and blind, public libraries, cybersecurity, technology modernization and the investigation of alleged educator misconduct. The agency said last week that it would release the second part of its request, for “categorical aid programs and other critical supports” for Wisconsin’s public schools, in November. The election is scheduled for Nov. 3. 
“The formula used for funding our schools, for years, has failed our children, schools and entire communities,” Underly said during her address. “The reasons are varied and complex, but you don’t need to be familiar with every detail of the funding formula to know that it’s simply not working. The evidence is all around us.” 
More than 75 school referendum requests carrying a total cost of $1.5 billion will go before voters in November. It’s just the latest round in a now-familiar ritual as school districts across the state  seek approval to raise property taxes to make up for a shrinking pool of  state aid. School districts that can’t pass a referendum have had to cut costs including by eliminating programs, staff and in some cases closing or consolidating schools. Districts on a streak of failed referendum requests have faced dissolution. 
Underly noted that the classrooms of the Hustisford School District “sat empty” on the first day of school this year. The district started the dissolution process after its referendum failed in April.
“Every kid felt the impact,” Underly said. “Kindergarteners, who should have been walking through the doors of the school their family chose when they made this beautiful community home, instead traveled to a neighboring town. Meanwhile, seniors who spent the past 12 years as Hustisford Falcons started their last year of school in an unfamiliar building,” Underly continued. “This is what happens when we turn our back on our schools. And when schools close, the impact doesn’t stop with students. It ripples through entire communities.”
Underly said the state funding formula “places value on the wrong things,” including enrollment, district spending and property value, instead of on student needs. 
“It fails to ask the most essential question: How much does it actually cost to educate the students who live in a district so that they have an equal opportunity to succeed? A student’s opportunity for success should not depend on their zip code,” she said. 
School funding will depend on who’s in office. Republican candidate Tom Tiffany and Democratic candidate David Crowley are running to be governor and control of the state Senate and Assembly are up for grabs. 
Some lawmakers have argued that rather than increase funding for schools the state needs to explore more school consolidation given declining enrollment. Asked about when school closure is the appropriate answer to declining enrollment, Underly told reporters she thinks “it deserves some study and conversation to figure out what’s best for kids.”
Underly pointed to the 2019 bipartisan Blue Ribbon Commission while speaking to reporters. The commission, which was created by Assembly Speaker Robin Vos and then-Senate Majority Leader Scott Fitzgerald in 2017, developed a report offering ideas to address school funding issues, as a guiding document for what the state should be doing. She said that the reports showed that there are kids who need additional support including those in poverty and who have special needs. She said money also needs to be invested in career and technical education, mental health supports and speech and language pathology.
“All these things have been in my past budget requests, and that’s what we will be able to expect in the next one, too,” Underly said. The agency’s 2024 state budget request totaled over  $4 billion. 
Urgent, but possibly not very fast
While Underly delivered her message with urgency, the timeline for changes could look vastly different depending on who wins in November.
Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein (D-Middleton), who could become the Senate Majority leader depending on the results of the November elections, has said Democrats will increase school funding in the next state budget, but changing the state’s school funding formula could be a “multi-year” process. 
“We’re also looking at a long-term goal of seeing what other states are doing and how they are funding their public schools, but that’s going to take probably a multi-year task to try to figure that all out and talking to our friends in Minnesota, Michigan, Illinois,” Hesselbein said. 
Crowley has been supportive of increasing school funding, including moving the state toward reimbursing districts for 90% of the cost of special education, instead of the current rate of 38% , but he has also suggested throughout his campaign for governor that there may need to be another Blue Ribbon Commission to study tax issues including school and local government funding. The last Blue Ribbon Commission on school funding took two years to complete. 
Tiffany has said he wants some increases to school funding, but also promises to freeze property taxes if elected. He hasn’t provided clarity on how much he would invest or how he would balance the two issues. Tiffany has focused on issues of accountability and ensuring “high standards” as opposed to school funding when discussing education issues.
Underly has had a strained relationship with Republicans on the Joint Finance Committee, who have declined to invite her to testify in front of the committee, and it’s unclear whether a working relationship between her and Tiffany would be an improvement. Tiffany recently described the state superintendent’s position as a constitutional office as a “problem” at a Moms For Liberty Town Hall in Richfield. He said he would use the state budget, which determines the state’s spending for a two-year period, to try to steer the superintendent  to make the decisions he wants her to make.
Underly said responding to the comments that independence is positive.  
“When you think about my office, my office is nonpartisan. It’s independent. It is not at the whim of any governor and I think that actually strengthens public education,” Underly said. “I think his comments stand on their own.”
In her speech, Underly called for people to look at the candidates’ records on school issues, not their talking points, when making their decisions at the ballot box this November. 
“We have people running for office who have spent a decade or more in government, in positions to make school funding decisions — or who have left state government for another level and now want to return — whose records include repeatedly voting against investments in Wisconsin’s children,” Underly said, apparently referring to Tiffany, who as a state lawmaker served on the budget committee before he was elected to Congress. “Past actions are the best evidence we have of what someone will do when given power again. Wisconsin does not need more people who tell us they support children while their votes tell a different story. We need people in positions of decision-making power who are pro-public school, pro-child and pro-Wisconsin.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Once again: Revenue growth through tax cuts is a mirage
description: Nearly two years ago, I wrote in this publication that the Kentucky General Assembly’s faith in income tax rate cuts as a vehicle for generating revenue was a mirage. At the time, the state was preparing to cut the individual income-tax rate from 4% to 3.5% even as revenue was expected to decline. I argued […]
text:
Kentucky has missed another trigger point in further lowering the state income tax. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Nearly two years ago, I wrote in this publication that the Kentucky General Assembly’s faith in income tax rate cuts as a vehicle for generating revenue was a mirage. At the time, the state was preparing to cut the individual income-tax rate from 4% to 3.5% even as revenue was expected to decline. I argued that Kentucky was making a dangerous bet that reducing one of the state’s most productive and reliable sources of revenue would somehow generate enough economic growth to replace what the tax cut surrendered.
Nearly two years later, members of the General Assembly have given us another opportunity to test that proposition. I’d truly like to say the results are encouraging; they unfortunately are not.
What the letter actually says
On Sept. 4, State Budget Director John Hicks sent a letter, the kind of letter that arrives at the office and immediately makes the rest of the day worse. Under KRS 141.020, General Fund receipts fell $1.19 billion short of what was required to trigger another cut in the individual income-tax rate. That’s not a rounding error, and that’s not a bad quarter. That’s over a billion dollars short of a target the General Assembly set.
And in case anyone was tempted to argue the bar was set too high, recall that floor was lowered further in 2025, building in a second, more forgiving trigger.  As a professor, we have a term for this, and it’s the fiscal equivalent of “grading on a curve.” Unfortunately, Kentucky missed that one too by slightly over $453 million. So, when you fail both the hard test and the easy test and get the same letter grade, it’s probably not the test that’s the problem.
This is no longer a theoretical debate anymore about the Laffer Curve or tax rate “sweet spot” as discussed in my original article. It’s an accounting problem, and accounting problems have an answer.
Here is what the Budget Director Hick’s letter does not say, but what its numbers make clear: this isn’t a state teetering on the edge of insolvency, unable to fund a tax cut because the cupboard is bare. The Budget Reserve Trust Fund commonly known as “Kentucky’s Rainy-Day Fund” sits at 26.1% of the General Fund, well over the 10% threshold the statute treats as healthy. The guardrails built are working exactly as designed. It’s just that what the revenue numbers are telling you isn’t what some folks were hoping to hear.
Arithmetic, not ideology
The General Assembly already reduced Kentucky’s individual income-tax rate from 5% to 3.5%, with the most recent cut taking effect Jan. 1 of this year. State revenue officials have acknowledged, in the same breath, that the reduction is itself contributing to declining individual income-tax receipts. That is not evidence that tax cuts are paying for themselves. It is evidence that tax cuts reduce tax revenue, which, respectfully, is not a controversial economic claim. It’s just plain arithmetic.
I suspect the response from some quarters of the General Assembly will be that the strategy isn’t the problem; it’s just we simply haven’t cut enough, or fast enough, and that the next cut is always the one that finally unleashes the growth the last several didn’t. Members of the General Assembly, that is precisely the trap you should decline to walk into a third time. At some point, chasing a mirage across the same stretch of desert stops being persistence and starts being a delusion you should probably examine.
Asking the right question 
There is nothing wrong with wanting a competitive tax structure, and nothing wrong with wanting Kentuckians to keep more of what they earn. But you cannot separate that goal from the other side of the ledger: what happens to the public investments the surrendered revenue would otherwise finance? The question in front of you was never “how quickly can we eliminate the income tax?” It should be “what tax structure gives Kentucky the resources it needs to become more prosperous?” Those are very different questions, and only one of them has an honest answer sitting in Director Hicks’s letter.
Economic growth doesn’t occur simply because government collects less money; it occurs when people and businesses have education, infrastructure, health care, public safety, and transportation systems that let them produce, invest, and innovate. A tax cut can put money in someone’s pocket. But if paying for it means underfunding the very investments that make growth possible, you haven’t created growth; you’ve just moved money from one pocket to another and charged Kentucky’s future for the privilege.
Guardrails, not gimmicks
So here is a recommendation, offered in the same spirit as nearly two years ago, only with better evidence behind it this time: keep the guardrails intact. Stop treating the income tax as though it were an economic development program with its own annual plan. Evaluate every tax expenditure and incentive on measurable results, not on how good it sounds in a press release. And if you really want to set Kentucky’s economy in the right direction, direct the state’s fiscal resources toward the things that actually expand Kentucky’s productive capacity like educational attainment, infrastructure, health care, workforce development, and strategic investment in Kentucky businesses, rather than a smaller tax code as an end in itself.

Nearly two years ago, I ended my column by warning that cutting the income tax from 4% to 3.5% amid declining revenue could prove reckless. Today, Kentucky’s own budget numbers, signed by the Commonwealth’s own budget director, provide the answer. The promised revenue growth has not materialized. The fiscal trigger has failed by more than a billion dollars under the first, more difficult test, and by nearly half a billion even under the test you relaxed to make it easier to pass.
Once again, you were forewarned nearly two years ago about the mirage, and it’s now high time to stop walking toward it.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana superintendents say they’re cutting jobs because of property tax reforms
description: Dozens of Indiana’s public school superintendents say their districts will cut teaching and support staff in the coming years to contend with the financial fallout of property tax reform, according to a new survey from the Indiana Coalition for Public Education. This is the second year the volunteer advocacy group surveyed superintendents about the financial[...]
text:
School buses wait for Indiana students on Aug. 6, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Dozens of Indiana’s public school superintendents say their districts will cut teaching and support staff in the coming years to contend with the financial fallout of property tax reform, according to a new survey from the Indiana Coalition for Public Education.
This is the second year the volunteer advocacy group surveyed superintendents about the financial outlook of their schools in the wake of Senate Enrolled Act 1, which set forth a series of major property tax reforms.
The survey went out to 290 superintendents throughout the state in August; 144 responded.
Other solutions raised in the report are creative: one superintendent said they planted prairie grass instead of mowing to save money on fuel; removed televisions to save on electricity and launched a student-run business to generate new income.
38 Indiana school districts to seek property tax referendums this fall

Nearly all of the respondents said they anticipate negative financial impacts from SEA 1, while a clear majority expressed similar concerns about universal school choice and the level of funding the General Assembly will allocate to public schools next year.
Schools would need anywhere from 1% to 25% in one-time funding increases to maintain the level of services expected by the community, plus an average of 6% in ongoing increases thereafter, the report found.
Jim May, a volunteer with the ICPE, described the findings as “more disheartening than surprising.”
“We’ve seen very large numbers of schools reduce staff, both support staff and teaching staff,” he said. “We’re seeing cuts to services. We’re seeing a lot of rural corporations saying things like classroom sizes are growing.”
How schools are contending with shortfalls?
Many districts are eliminating support staff and teaching roles to make up for budget shortfalls.
Half of respondents said they’ve already cut support staff, while another 16% will do so soon and 30% are considering the same.
Forty-six percent of superintendents said they are eliminating some teaching roles. That number rises to 93% when accounting for districts that are actively considering or will take similar action.
Nearly 40% have issued or will issue a new general obligation bond, though many others are considering the option to raise more support.
Others are considering delayed maintenance, reduced staff raises, cuts to transportation services, electives and field trips or consolidation. One raised the possibility their district won’t be able to sustain student internships, career pathways or dual-credit offerings.
In rural districts, superintendents say they worry lawmakers are pressuring them to consolidate or close schools.
“I feel like funding is bleeding the small schools dry,” one superintendent wrote. “I am skeptical that this is simply a push to consolidate.”
“Our commitment to live within our means in the past, with no referendum and super low tax rates, has caught up with us,” another said. “I think larger schools with better tax bases have given the rest of us a black eye. We haven’t spent haphazardly, but are punished like we did.”
Story continues below
ICPE_2026-School-Funding-Report
 
Why so few referendums?
Far fewer districts are seeking a referendum than initially expected this year, despite it being a record year for referendum questions on the ballot.
Responses to the group’s superintendent survey offer a clue as to why so few took this route: 39% of respondents cited a lack of support within their communities.
This is particularly true for rural districts, which were more likely to cut staff than pursue a referendum when compared to urban and suburban districts.
Still, survey responses suggest more referendums could appear on the ballot in 2028 — the next year schools can do so.
“We cannot continue to do more with less,” one superintendent wrote in response to the survey, which did not identify respondents. 
“Funding has got to keep pace with salary requirements, safety concerns, increased utility costs, and increased equipment and supply costs. In a day and age where we are required to do more and more to support our students and their families, we lack the financial support to do so. At some point in the very near future we will all have no choice to run a referendum because of the inadequate financial support. And on top of all of those increased costs, in my district 51% of our students do not have English as their native language — it does take more to educate them.”
Others lamented the state’s move to universal access for private school vouchers, which became available to all Hoosier families regardless of income for the first time this year.
Braun touts start of universal school choice in Indiana

“It is a shame that our Indiana public schools are being unnecessarily defunded by our general assembly,” one superintendent wrote, saying they were advised to eliminate $2.5 million from the district’s budget.
“Our state’s super majority has chosen to create a manufactured financial crisis by way of funding their voucher program, supporting the growth of their charter school program, and the growth of statewide online schools/platforms. Billions of dollars are being funneled away from our public schools to support these private projects.”
Several respondents suggested private schools should be subject to similar accountability measures as public schools as a condition to accept publicly-funded vouchers.
One superintendent went a step further, suggesting any new or existing law should apply to equally to public and private schools supported by tax dollars.
“I do not believe it was a wise financial decision to prioritize paying for the private education of wealthy families,” the superintendent wrote. 
“That said, the decision has been made and Indiana is now a 100% school choice state. If this is the case, then we need to level the playing field so all school entities are operating on a level playing field. Any current or new law that applies to public education should be applied to any other school system that accepts state dollars.”
